gent-jenkins-muskogee-1915-08.A1:
HATCHET FIEND
IS AGAIN BUSY
IN MUSKOGEE
MERCHANT ATTACKED IN HIS STORE DIES FROM WOUNDS, AFTER SAYING IT WAS ACT OF WHITE MAN.
Muskogee, Okla., Aug. 11.—W. B. Province, a grocer, was attacked by a murderer with a hatchet in Province's store shortly after noon Wednesday and three hours later died of his wounds. His last breath was spent as he murmured that a white man had struck the blow.

The crime was discovered shortly after one o'clock, when Province's wife entered the store, which is on the outskirts of the city. She saw her husband leaning weakly against a counter, blood flowing freely from several wounds. A closer examination showed that Province had been struck first in the back of the head and finally his face had been hacked by several blows from the hatchet. This weapon was found on the floor by the man's side.

A scoop half full of lard and the position of Province near the barrel containing lard, leads officers to believe that the assailant entered the store, asked for lard and struck the first blow while the grocer had his back turned, bending over the barrel.

Police officials arrested a negro who gave the name of J. Jenkins only a few minutes after the murder was discovered, but he was afterwards released. A woman who lived directly across the street from Province's store declares she saw a negro enter during the noon hour, but the dying man's last statement has caused officers to believe that the negro is not the murderer.

Province was rushed to a hospital and operated upon but to no avail. It is believed that robbery was the only motive for the murder since the cash drawer was riffled. The murder is the third due to hatchet hends occurring in this city in little more than a year, and the fifth occurring in Muskogee county in the same time. In none of the cases has a single person been brought to justice.
gent-jenkins-muskogee-1915-08.A2:
MURDER MOST FOUL
Last Wednesday the fiend known as the hatchet fiend got busy and another murder was committed Mr. Wm B. Province a white man who runs a gracery at 22nd and Okmulgee was the victim. Several arrests it is claimed were made and among the number was a negro, Gent Jenkins who was afterward discharged who ever the guilty fiend is be he white black or red should be purnished as the law directs.

Soon after the arrest of Jinkins there was armor started that a lynching be proposed but the officers of the law Chief of Police Depew and his farce and Sheriff Barger and his Deputies able re-inforced by the sentiment of the best class of white and colored citizens let it be known that a mob gathering would be furnishing lots of material for the undertaker and the embryo mob dissolved. We are proud of the good citizenship of Muskogee because from the beginning up to this date they have always stood as a remit against mob violence.
gent-jenkins-muskogee-1915-08.A3:
MURDERER'S AX IDENTIFIED
Muskogee Authorities Say Arrest for Murder is Expected.
Muskogee, Okla., Aug. 14.—The old rusty hand-ax with its crude handle, used by a brutal assassin to take the life of William B. Province, a suburban grocer, Wednesday, was identified today and removed from the show window of a downtown store, where the police had placed it for that purpose. Just where this identification leads, the officers will not disclose at this time, but say that an arrest will probably be made in the next few days.

County Attorney Branson this afternoon held a secret court of inquisition, questioning about forty witnesses. Among those summoned was the widow of Province.
gent-jenkins-muskogee-1915-08.A6:
WOMAN HELD
FOR MURDER
OF HUSBAND
WIFE OF GROCERYMAN SLAIN WITH HATCHET AT MUSKO GEE, ACCUSED OF MURDER INSTRUMENT IDENTIFIED.
Muskogee, Okla., Sept. 2.—Charged with the "hatchet murder" of her husband, W. B. Province, the suburban grocer killed in his store at midday on August 11 last, Mrs. Province, the widow, was arrested Thursday afternoon on a warrant sworn out and authorized by County Attorney Fred P. Branson.

The arrest of Mrs. Province came only after officers had pleaded for days with the county attorney to take this course and after a sensational identification of the hatchet used to kill the grocer—the hatchet which Mrs. Province swore before the coroner's inquest, did not belong to the store.

Two days ago former Deputy Sheriff W. L. Robbins telephoned Branson stating that his 14-year-old boy had played with the Province boys for a long time and would probably be able to tell whether or not the hatchet belonged at the store.

Thursday morning Branson secured two old, rusty hatchets and the hatchet found after the murder. He put the three hatchets together in the waste basket of his office. When young Robbins was brought to the office, Branson asked him if he could swear positively that he had seen a hatchet on the Province place.

"I can," said the boy, "and I would know it."

"Well, if that is so," said Branson, pulling the hatchets from their hiding place and laying them on the floor "tell me if all of these or any of these is the hatchet you have seen and if so point out all or any that you have seen on the Province place."

"This is the one," said the boy, without a second's hesitation, as he reached down and picked up the hatchet which was found by officers in the store after Province had been murdered.

Three adults also have sworn positively that they have noticed a hatchet at the Province place, but none have made such a positive identification as the boy. To offset this testimony there are statements by at least two people that there was no hatchet at the Province store.

Ever since the day of the murder many officers, as well as Pinkerton detectives especially employed on the case, and many people living near the Province home on Twenty-sixth and Okmulgee streets, have requested Eranson to arrest the woman, but until Thursday afternoon he stood firm in his refusal.

"There has been evidence," said Eranson only a few minutes after the
Branson only a few minutes after the warrant was issued, "that Mrs. Province has left her husband upon one occasion, that she has been quarreling with him over many matters, and it has been called to my attention that her mind may have been affected at different periods in life."

It is understood that Branson, the sheriff's force and police officers who have been quietly working on the case ever since the murder have accumulated a mass of evidence which, however, will not be given out at this time. One piece of this evidence is said to be a contradiction of Mrs. Province's statement that she was in the tomato patch adjoining the grocery store just before her husband was murdered. The time was shortly after a rain that left the ground soggy but after a careful examination by two officers that same afternoon failed to reveal to them any tracks in the garden.

Pleads Not Guilty.

Mrs. Province was brought to the justice court of W. G. Miller, where she has been arraigned, pleading not guilty.

Dressed in a black gown which she has worn since the day after her husband's murder, Mrs. Province interrupted while Justice Miller was reading her the charge, to plead "not guilty." Her voice was calm and apparently she was little disturbed.

jacob-brooks-alexandria-1915-08-22.A2:
Special Officer Shot and Killed Negro
Who Was Assaulting
Him
A coronor's jury summoned by Dr. T. Marshall Jones, city coronor, held an inquest at 11 o'clock this morning over the remains of Jacob Brooks, colored, who was shot and instantly killed yesterday afternoon by Henry Allen, special officer at the plant of the Alexandria Fertilizer and Chemical Co. Allen was exonorated by the Jury.

The shooting of Brooks who lives at 404 Oronoco street, followed an attack made by him on the officer when he atttempted to place him under arrest. According to Allen's testimony Brooks was fighting with a woman named Martha Myers near the chemical plant yesterday and the man had knocked the woman down and was kicking her on the side when he interfered and placed the couple under arrest. He had proceeded but a short distance on north Lee street with his prisoners when Brooks jerked the heavy hickory baton from the officer's hand and made an attack on him. Allen said that he warded off several blows with his left arm, and when the man finally landed a blow on his head he drew his revolver and fired twice. In the meanwhile the woman had jerked loose and hurried bricks at Allen's head.

Allen was taken to the Alexandria Hospital where Dr. Arthur Snowden took five stitches in his head. Shortly after the shooting the woman was arrested by Sergeant Wilkerson and policeman Reid and Snollings land locked up.

After hearing the evidence of several witnesses the coroner's jury returned the following verdict: "That Jacob Brooks came to his death from a pistol shot fired by Special Officer Henry Allen while on duty and having said Brooks under arrest, the shot being fired in self defense, Brooks having seized his billy and attacked him, the said Allen, and we hereby exonorate the said Allen."

The jury was composed of C. J. W. Summers, foreman; A. G. Uhler, P. M. Bradshaw, J F. Lowenbach, R. C. Reeves and C. Page Waller, Jr.
jacob-brooks-alexandria-1915-08-22.A3:
SUNDAY'S
TRAGEDY
The killing of a negro by a special officer late Sunday on North Lee Street made the sixth member of that race shot to death by officers in this city during past years. In 1886 a desperate negro was killed by an officer near the northwest corner of Princess and Fairfax streets. Later an officer was forced to shoot two negroes at the old Fayette street depot. One died almost as soon as shot and the other lingered but a short time. A few years later another of that race met his death near Spring Park while endeavoring to shoot officers who were pursuing him. Another tragedy followed close in the wake of the latter, when a desperate negro, who was armed, took up a position behind a stone wall a short distance north of Spring Park. In addition to the above two men were shot by an officer on the Strand a few years ago. They were brothers and had been engaged in a fight with a man. When the officer appeared and attempted to place the brothers under arrest they resisted and were getting the better of the minion of the law when the latter drew his pistol and shot both. One died almost immediately, but the other survived his wound and lived several years after the shooting.
jacob-brooks-alexandria-1915-08-22.A4:
SAYS HE KILLED
IN SELF-DEFENSE
Alexandria Watchman Who
Shot Negro Is Acquitted
by Jury.
MANY FINES COLLECTED
Police Court Takes in $105 as the Result of Two Poker Raids.
Alexandria, Va., Aug. 23.—Henry Allen, a special watchman employed at the plant of the Alexandria Fertilizer and Chemical Company, who yesterday shot and killed Jacob Brooks, colored, was exonerated today by a coroner's jury summoned by Dr. T. M. Jones, which met at Wheatley's undertaking establishment and heard the evidence in the case.

In its verdict the jury set forth that Brooks was under arrest at the time and that the policeman shot in self-defense, Brooks having seized Allen's billy and attacked him.

The jury was composed of the following: C. J. W. Summers, foreman; A. G. Uhler, secretary; P., M. Bradshaw, Joseph Lowebach, C. Page Waller and R. C. Reeves.

Allen was the first to testify. He said he saw Brooks and Martha Miles engaged in a quarrel, which was followed by a fight. When he interfered Brooks struck him on the head and arm. He grabbed his pistol and pulled the trigger. After the first shot Brooks advanced and Allen fired a second shot, Brooks falling and dying a few minutes afterward. Allen told the jury that the reason he shot was that he was afraid his life was in danger.
Fines aggregating $105 were collected in the Police Court today as the result of two poker raids made Saturday by the police. This included two men who appeared and were fined $10 each for interfering with the police in making a raid and one fined for abusive language, who also was fined $10.

Henry Schlichting, who conducts a place on the west side of Royal street, between King and Cameron streets, forfeited $20 collateral, and eight others, also charged with unlawful gambling, forfeited $5 collateral each.

John E. Henderson and George Beard were charged with interfering with the officers when they entered Schlichting's place and were fined $10 each.

The five captured in the raid of a poolroom at the northeast corner of Duke and Henry streets forfeited $5 collateral each, and Arthur Welch, arrested after the raid, charged with abusive language, forfeited $10 collateral.

Alice Kitts, colored, whose place the police raided, and seven others, who were charged with disorderly conduct, were acquitted. The police testified that a piano was being played late and there was also dancing in progress.

The proposed fight to test the Constitutionality of the State law requiring the payment of omitted taxes was discussed at length tonight by the Retail Merchants' Association at a meeting held in the rooms of the chamber of commerce.

At a mass meeting of the retailers of the city held recently it was decided to test the law requiring the payment of omitted taxes. This was also discussed by the wholesale merchants, who will join the retailers in the fight. Attorney H. Noel Garner has been retained by the retail merchants; Attorney Garner L. Boothe will appear for the wholesale merchants, and Attorney James R. Caton, a former member of the State legislature, will be associated with both attorneys. According to a notice recently sent the merchants the time limit for making reports to Examiner W. N. Lipscomb expires August 26.

The marriage of Alfred C. Moss, teller at the Alexandria National Bank, and Miss Bessie Lambert, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Charles Lambert, Staunton, Va., took place Saturday. Mr. and Mrs. Moss are spending their honeymoon at Old Point Comfort, Va. They will reside in this city.

Many matters of importance are slated for the semi-monthly meeting of the City Council Tuesday night.

Mrs. Alice G. Poss' funeral will take place at 5 o'clock Tuesday afternoon from her late home, 1109 King street. Services will be conducted by Rev. Dr. W. F. Watson, pastor of the First Baptist Church.

The funeral of Michael Creegan will take place at 9 o'clock Tuesday morning from St. Mary's Catholic Church. Burial will be in St. Mary's Cemetery.

A chicken supper will be given from 5 until 9 o'clock Tuesday evening in the parish hall of St. Rita's Catholic Church, Mount Ida, Alexandria County.

A moonlight excursion was given tonight by the Young Men's Sodality Lyceum on the steamer St. John's.

jacob-brooks-alexandria-1915-08-22.A5:
WATCHMAN SHOOTS
MARAUDING NEGRO
Alexandria, Va., Aug. 23.—Henry Allen, a special watchman employed by the Alexandria Fertilizer and Chemical Company, shot and killed Jacob Brooks, colored, after Brooks had been placed under arrest for attacking the watchman with the latter's stick.

The shooting took place in Lee Street, between Queen and Princess. Two shots were fired by Allen, both bullets entering the right side about the lung. Brooks died almost instantly.

Allen was attracked by a fight between Brooks and Martha Myers, colored, nineteen years old. Brooks was beating the woman and had knocked her down. Allen, who has full police power, placed both under arrest. They broke away from him and Allen says Brooks grabbed his hickory walking stick which he carries while making his rounds and beat him over the head, face and arms, while the Myers woman threw bricks at him. Allen then fired.

Allen's face was covered with blood from the injuries he received and he was taken to the Alexandria Hospital, where four stitches were taken by Drs. Moore and Snowden. He will remain at the hospital until tomorrow.

The body of Brooks was removed to Wheatley's undertaking establishment, where an inquest probably will be held tomorrow by Coroner T. M. Jones, who arrived on the scene a short time after the shooting.

Chief Goods, Sergeant Wilkinson, and Policeman Snellings and Reid arrived on the scene of the affair a short time afterward and started an investigation, resulting in the arrest of Martha Myers, who is charged on the blotter at police headquarters with disorderly conduct and fighting. The woman admitted at police station tonight that Brooks was beating her.

Brooks was about forty years old, and lived at 404 Oronoco Street. He had a wife and two children and was employed by the Mutual Ice Company.

jacob-brooks-alexandria-1915-08-22.A8:
Sheriff Outwits Mob.
Murphysboro, Ill.—A mob of several hundred persons who surrounded the Harrisburg, Ill, jail, intent on lynching Joe DeBerry, a colored man, who will be tried for the murder of a white woman, were outwitted by a sheriff's party last week. DeBerry was smuggled out of the Harrisburg jail and under the protection of three companies of Illinois State Militia was brought here and placed in the local jail.

Alexandria, Va.—Henry Allen, special officer for the Alexandria Fertilizer Co., shot and instantly killed Jacob Brooks, colored, of 404 Oronoca street, Alexandria. Brooks had words with Martha Myers and had assaulted her. The officer spoke to him and Brooks attacked Allen, who drew his revolver and shot him dead.
